verses.translation_literal: And Elijah the Tishbite, [one] of the dwellers of Gilead, said to Ahab: Living [is] YHWH, the God of Israel, before whose face I stand—if there will be [during] these years dew and rain, except at the mouth of my word!
verses.translation_dramatic: Out of nowhere—out of the rugged uplands of Gilead, beyond the Jordan—a man stands before Ahab. Elijah: his very name a creed, my God is the LORD. Elijah the Tishbite, one of the sojourners of Gilead, a man of no standing and no father the story troubles to name. He does not ask leave to speak. He swears, and the oath hangs in the air between them: “As the LORD lives, the God of Israel, before whom I stand—there will be no dew and no rain in these years. None. Not unless I say the word.”
verses.directors_commentary:
Elijah arrives with no call story, no genealogy and no warning, and his first act is an oath to a king who has just brought Baal worship in from Sidon (1 Kings 16:31–33). The target is exact. Dew and rain were Baal’s portfolio: in the Ugaritic myths he is the Rider on the Clouds, dew is personified as his daughter Ṭallay, and when he goes down into death the land dries. To swear “as the LORD lives” while cancelling both says that the living God holds the sky. In a country with a rainless summer, dew carries the crops from the last spring rain to the first autumn one, so “no dew nor rain” shuts the whole farming year; Malbim adds that the Torah’s drought-curse (Deut 11:17) never mentions dew, so Elijah goes beyond the book. “Before whom I stand” is courtier’s language: a servant of a higher king addressing a lower one.

The KJV smooths three things. “There shall not be dew nor rain” turns an oath into a forecast: the Hebrew is the broken oath formula, literally “if there will be dew and rain …”, the self-curse left unsaid, and the silence is the threat. “Who was of the inhabitants of Gilead” adds “who was” and flattens tôšābê, “resident aliens”, men living on another’s land; the word chimes with “the Tishbite” (hattišbî … mittôšābê), a sound-pun English loses. “According to my word” hides a body part: lĕpî dĕbārî is “at the mouth of my word”, which sets up the chapter’s question of whose word this really is (vv. 2, 5, 8, 16, 24). Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David explain the abruptness through 1 Kings 16:34: Hiel’s sons died as Joshua had cursed (Josh 6:26), Ahab scoffed that Joshua’s curse held while Moses’s drought warning (Deut 11:16–17) did not, and Elijah swore. That is rabbinic story, not text.

philological_notes.note: “One of the resident aliens of.” A tôšāb is a settler without land or full citizenship, dependent on a host community (cf. Lev 25:23, 35). The sound echoes “the Tishbite” (hattišbî) just before it, and the root yšb returns when Elijah “dwells” at Kerith (v. 5) and is told to “dwell” at Zarephath (v. 9). Radak, following Targum Jonathan, takes the Tishbite as a man from a town called Tishbe who then took up residence in Gilead; Metzudat Zion stresses that he had lived in Gilead a long time.

“Living is YHWH” is the standard oath. The ʾim-clause that follows is the oath’s self-curse cut short (“may I be struck if …”), so “if there will be dew and rain” means “there will surely be none”; kî ʾim then means “except”. STEPBible’s “that … except” splits the pair; together they mean “except”. The same oath form is spoken back to Elijah by the widow in v. 12.

Literally “to the mouth of my word.” lĕpî, “according to the mouth of”, is a measure or command (Gen 47:12, lĕpî haṭṭāp, “according to the little ones”). Elijah claims rain will move only when his word moves it. Targum Jonathan has “unless when I say”; Radak adds “by God’s command”; Metzudat David reads it as the length of time Elijah speaks in prayer; Malbim makes the boast the point: the drought rests on Elijah’s own decree, not on the Torah’s automatic covenant curse.

token_glosses.gloss: one of the resident aliens (dwellers) of

verses.translation_literal: And the word of YHWH was to him, saying:
verses.translation_dramatic: And then the word of the LORD came to him—not an idea, an event—and it said:
verses.directors_commentary: The narrator’s formula for a prophetic message is “the word of YHWH was to him.” The verb is a plain “was/happened”, and dābār means both “word” and “event, thing”, so the word is reported as something that occurs to a person, not something he thinks. Note the order: Elijah has already sworn in his own voice (v. 1), and only now does the text give him a word to obey. Radak (on “by my word”) closes the gap by saying God had already told him to show himself to Ahab and that rain would follow; the reader learns to hear God’s word inside Elijah’s “my word”. The KJV’s “came unto him” is a fair rendering; YLT’s “is unto him” shows the flat Hebrew “was”. The identical sentence opens verse 8, which sets the chapter’s two commissions, Kerith (vv. 2–7) and Zarephath (vv. 8–24), as matched panels.

philological_notes.note: “The word of YHWH.” dābār is both “word” and “thing, event”, so the formula reports an occurrence, not a thought. It is the keyword of the chapter: Elijah’s “my word” (v. 1), the word he obeys (vv. 5, 8), the word he speaks to the widow (vv. 14–16), and the closing “the word of YHWH in your mouth is truth” (v. 24).

verses.translation_literal: Go from this [place], and turn for yourself eastward, and hide yourself in the wadi of Kerith, which [is] upon the face of the Jordan.
verses.translation_dramatic: “Go from this place. Turn your face to the sunrise and go to ground—hide yourself in the wadi of Kerith, the one that looks out upon the Jordan.”
verses.directors_commentary: Why hide? A man who has just sworn a drought in the king’s face has committed what any ancient court would call a capital offence. The text says only “hide”; Rashi supplies “from Ahab and Jezebel”, Metzudat David “so that Ahab does not kill you”, and Obadiah later says Ahab searched every nation and kingdom for him (18:10). The direction carries weight too: Hebrew orients by the sunrise, so qēdmâ means “eastward” and “forward” at once, and Elijah turns his back on the cultivated west for the wilds of the Transjordan. The KJV blurs two words. “Brook” suggests a perennial English stream; a naḥal is a wadi, a winter watercourse that runs only after rain, which is exactly what fails in verse 7. And “before Jordan” reads in modern English like “this side of”, but ʿal-pĕnê means “facing, east of”; the site is disputed (Transjordan, or Wadi Qelt near Jericho). The name Kerith probably comes from kārat, “to cut”, a gorge cut in the rock; in 18:4 Jezebel is “cutting off” (hakrît) the LORD’s prophets, so the hiding-place and the persecution share a root.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of “hide”: “hide yourself” or “be hidden”, with God left as a possible hand behind the passive. Rashi gives the danger (Ahab and Jezebel) and Radak the aim (that no one know where he is). Malbim ties the hiding to the biblical idea of God hiding his face from Israel (Deut 31:17): the prophet who withholds the rain is himself withdrawn from view.

“Eastward”, with the directional ending -âh. The root means “front”: the Hebrew compass faces the sunrise, so front is east and behind (ʾāḥôr) is west. Note also the consonantal pun in the verse: lēk, “go”, and lĕkā, “for yourself”, are both written לך.

Literally “upon the face of the Jordan”: “facing” or “east of” it. KJV’s “before Jordan” is ambiguous at best in modern English. Metzudat David reads the wadi as lying east of the Jordan; Targum Jonathan keeps the Hebrew phrase word for word.

verses.translation_literal: And it will be [that] from the wadi you will drink; and the ravens I have commanded to sustain you there.
verses.translation_dramatic: “You will drink from the wadi. And the ravens—the ravens!—I have given them their orders. They will keep you fed there.”
verses.directors_commentary: The sentence is built for surprise. The object is thrown to the front, “and the ravens—I have commanded”, so the listener hears “ravens” before anything else; the KJV’s “I have commanded the ravens to feed thee” buries it. Ravens are unclean birds (Lev 11:15), carrion-eaters, the bird Noah sent out first, so food carried by them is itself a test of Elijah’s scruples (Ralbag and Metzudat David take it up). Metzudat David also hears a lesson in mercy (if cruel ravens pity him, he must pity Israel); Malbim turns it round (the cruel birds remind him of his own cruelty to a starving people). “Feed” under-translates kilkēl, “to sustain, provision”, the verb of Joseph supplying his family in famine (Gen 47:12) and of Solomon’s officers provisioning the king’s table (1 Kgs 4:7): Elijah is put on royal rations. And the water is only as sure as the rain, because this “brook” is a wadi.

philological_notes.note: “The ravens”, which Metzudat Zion glosses simply as “the black birds”. Radak takes them as real ravens, whose hearts God moved to bring food twice a day, and records the rabbinic alternatives that they carried it from Ahab’s or from Jehoshaphat’s table, or that ʿōrĕbîm were “merchants”, as in ʿōrĕbê maʿărābēk. The pointed text means ravens, and I follow it.

“To sustain you”: a reduplicated (polel) stem of the root “contain, hold”. It is the verb of household and royal provisioning, not just “feeding”. Metzudat Zion defines it as “supplying of food”. It returns for the widow in v. 9, so the same promise is made twice, first with ravens and then with the poorest woman in Sidon.
“I have commanded”: the ravens are given an order like servants of a household. Metzudat David and Radak both read it as “I have put it in their heart”, the instinct made obedience.

verses.translation_literal: And he went, and he did according to the word of YHWH; and he went, and he dwelt in the wadi of Kerith, which [is] upon the face of the Jordan.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he went—he did just as the word of the LORD had said. He went, and he took up his dwelling in the wadi of Kerith, there where it faces the Jordan.
verses.directors_commentary: The Hebrew is almost liturgical: “he went and he did according to the word of YHWH; and he went and he dwelt.” The doubled “and he went” is deliberate: the first clause states the obedience in general, the second repeats it to say what it was concretely. The KJV’s “So … for” adds two connectives that are not there and turns a repetition into an argument. The obedience formula returns when the widow, told to bake for Elijah first, “goes and does according to the word of Elijah” (v. 15), so obedience passes from God to prophet to widow. Notice the verb too: the man introduced in v. 1 as a tôšāb, a “dweller”, who “stands” before YHWH, now “dwells” (wayyēšeb), the same root, as if the label were being lived out. Malbim finds two acts here, one visible (the move to the Jordan) and one hidden (heaven’s attention turned to the border), the second signalled by “he did”.

philological_notes.note: “And he dwelt” (or “sat”). The same root as tôšābê, “the resident aliens of” Gilead (v. 1), and as wĕyāšabtā, “and dwell there” (v. 9): the sojourner is made to sojourn.
“He did according to the word of YHWH”: the obedience formula. Malbim reads “he did” as a hidden act in the upper realms, set against the visible “he went and dwelt”.

verses.translation_literal: And the ravens [were] bringing to him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and from the wadi he would drink.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so the days settled into their pattern. The ravens came—black wings against the first light—bringing him bread and meat. They came again at evening, bringing bread and meat. And from the wadi he drank.
verses.directors_commentary: The grammar paints a routine, not an event: the subject is fronted (“and the ravens”), the verb is a participle (“were bringing”), and “he would drink” is habitual. The KJV’s plain past, “brought … drank”, reads like a single delivery. The promise of verse 4 is reported back in reverse order, promised “wadi, ravens”, delivered “ravens, wadi”. Look at what he eats: bread and meat, twice a day. In a village economy meat was feast-day food, so this is royal-table fare for a fugitive; Radak preserves a tradition that the ravens carried it from Ahab’s or Jehoshaphat’s table. KJV “flesh” is just the old word for meat, though a modern ear hears worse; bāśār is meat. On ritual purity, Metzudat David says that since the LORD told him to eat, he knew the meat was kosher. The English versions split here: the BBE has “bread in the morning and meat in the evening”, which appears to follow the Greek and would echo the manna-and-quail pattern of Exodus 16:8, 12; the Masoretic text doubles both, and I keep it.

philological_notes.note: A Hiphil participle of “come”, so “bringing”: continuing or repeated action. It sets the ravens’ service as a routine with no end in sight, which prepares the “end of days” of v. 7.

“And meat.” Eating meat delivered by an unclean bird raised the question of kashrut. Metzudat David answers that God’s command to eat showed it was fit; Ralbag adds that prophecy can set aside a commandment, so there was no sin.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, from the end of days, [that] the wadi dried up, for there had not been rain in the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then the days ran down, as days do. At the end of them the wadi dried up—the very water he drank—for no rain had fallen in the land. The drought he had sworn into being had come to the place where he hid.
verses.directors_commentary: The prophet’s own word reaches him first. The narrator does not say “because of Elijah’s oath”; he gives the flat cause, “there had been no rain in the land”, and lets the reader connect it. Everything depends on what naḥal means. A wadi is a seasonal channel, full after the winter rains and dry by summer; the KJV’s “brook” suggests a perennial stream, so the drying looks like a second miracle when it is only hydrology. “From the end of days” (miqqēṣ yāmîm) is a time-idiom; the KJV’s “after a while” is fair, though in some uses “days” means a full year. The narrator also changes the word for rain: Elijah swore by māṭār (v. 1), while the cause given here is geshem, the heavy winter downpour that actually fills wadis; the KJV reads both as “rain”. Rashi takes the drying as pressure from God: Elijah should feel the need for rain, since Israel’s hunger was hard in God’s eyes.

philological_notes.note: “From the end of days”: an idiom for an unspecified stretch of time, as in Gen 4:3. Targum Jonathan renders it “from the end of days” as well. In some contexts “days” means a full year, so this may mark a full turn of the seasons.
“The wadi”: a seasonal valley or watercourse, running with or without a stream (BDB: “wady”). The word is what makes verse 7 natural, not miraculous: wadis die when the rain does.
“Rain”, but the heavy winter shower or downpour, a different word from the māṭār of v. 1. It is the rain that fills wadis; its absence is what dries Kerith.

verses.translation_literal: And the word of YHWH was to him, saying:
verses.translation_dramatic: Then—once more—the word of the LORD came to him, and it said:
verses.directors_commentary: Word for word the formula of verse 2, and the hinge between the chapter’s two panels. Note what is missing: when the wadi fails Elijah does not pray, complain or ask, at least not in the text. The narrator reports the drying (v. 7) and the next word arrives unrequested. Rashi’s reading of verse 7 is that this is what the drying was for. The KJV renders the repetition identically, as it should; the Hebrew “was” again gives the word as an event.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, go to Zarephath, which [belongs] to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded there a woman, a widow, to sustain you.
verses.translation_dramatic: “Arise, and go. To Zarephath, in the country of Sidon—and dwell there. Behold: there I have commanded a woman, a widow, to sustain you.”
verses.directors_commentary: Where God sends him is the point. Zarephath “belongs to Sidon”, the home country of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians and father of Jezebel, whose marriage brought Baal worship to Israel’s court (1 Kgs 16:31). The prophet who has just cancelled Baal’s rain is sent to hide on Baal’s own ground, and the drought, as the next verses show, is there too. Ralbag adds that the phrase tells this Zarephath from the one named in Obadiah 20. The KJV’s “widow woman” is a sound rendering of the Hebrew apposition “a woman, a widow”; what it loses is the paradox. A widow was the poorest person in the ancient economy (no husband, no inheritance, dependent on gleanings and charity; Deut 24:19–21 reserves them for the foreigner, the orphan and the widow), and this one is a foreigner. God’s “command” is not something she knows she has received. Radak and Ralbag stress that she has nothing, so the supply must be a miracle; Rashi says the command was issued “in my heavenly retinue”; Malbim says she was a righteous woman. “Arise, go” is the same pair God speaks to Jonah (Jonah 1:2), and Radak records the midrash that this widow was Jonah’s mother.

philological_notes.note: “To Zarephath” (Greek Sarepta), a Phoenician coastal town, with the directional ending -âh. The name looks like ṣārap, “to smelt, refine”, which may foreshadow the testing of the widow; that is my own reading. Ralbag says the added “which belongs to Sidon” distinguishes it from another Zarephath (Obad 20); Metzudat David simply calls it a city in the land of Sidon.

“A woman, a widow”: two nouns in apposition, an indefinite figure, the legal and economic category of one without a male provider. Radak and Ralbag both argue that she had nothing to sustain him with, so the command can only mean a miracle; Malbim holds that she was righteous enough to be worth a blessing.
“I have commanded there.” Rashi: “in my retinue” (bĕpamalyâ šellî), the order issued in the heavenly court, not to her. Metzudat David: “I have appointed there a woman, a widow.”

verses.translation_literal: And he arose and went to Zarephath, and he came to the entrance of the city, and behold, there [was] a woman, a widow, gathering sticks; and he called to her and said: Take, please, for me a little water in the vessel, and let me drink.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he arose and went to Zarephath, under a sky that had stopped giving. At the entrance to the city—there! A woman. A widow, stooping to gather sticks. He called out to her: “Take—please—a little water for me, in a vessel, that I may drink.”
verses.directors_commentary:
Elijah was told “a widow”, not which one, so the Hebrew introduces her as any stranger is met: “behold, there—a woman, a widow”, indefinite. The KJV’s “the widow woman” quietly gives Elijah a recognition he may not have. The commentators split: Rashi has him unsure, and, like Abraham’s servant at the well (Gen 24), setting a sign: the woman who gives me water is she; Malbim has him recognise her and probe what she lacks, beginning with water. The scene is the old well-scene turned over. A stranger asks a woman for “a little water” (the very words of Gen 24:17), but she is no bride; she is a widow gleaning twigs outside the walls, and what follows is a funeral meal, not a wedding. Hospitality to a stranger was the basic duty of the Near East, and water the cheapest gift; in a drought, to ask it of the poorest person in town is a test.

A further point for the KJV audit: the Hebrew uses one verb, “take” (qĕḥî here, and again in v. 11), where the KJV varies it to “fetch” and “bring”, and the BBE turns the imperative-with-please into a question (“Will you give me …?”). And “gathering sticks” is qôšēš, picking up twigs and stubble, not felling timber (Metzudat Zion): the fuel of the destitute.

philological_notes.note: “Gathering”: qôšēš is the picking up of thin small things, stubble or twigs; Metzudat Zion cites Exod 5:12, “to gather stubble”. As far as I can tell, the only other place the Bible has the exact phrase mĕqōšēš ʿēṣîm is Num 15:32–33, the man found gathering wood on the Sabbath; here it signals poverty, not an offence.

“And behold, there—a woman, a widow”: indefinite, so the reader meets her as Elijah does. Malbim notes that “there” does not mean she lived at the gate: she happened to be there, prepared by God so that Elijah would find her as he arrived. Rashi has Elijah not recognising her.

“Take, please, for me”: a polite imperative. Metzudat David reads it as “take from your house and bring to me”. The verb is “take”, repeated in v. 11 (lāqaḥat, liqḥî), and it is the thread of the scene.

verses.translation_literal: And she went to take [it]; and he called to her and said: Take, please, for me a morsel of bread in your hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: She went to take it—and as she went he called out to her again: “Take for me, please, a morsel of bread. In your hand.”
verses.directors_commentary: The first request cost her nothing: she goes, and not a word of hers is told. The second is the one that will break the scene. Water is the cheapest duty of hospitality; bread is a household’s whole supply. He asks for a pat leḥem, “a morsel of bread”, the formula of polite understatement, as when Abraham says he will fetch “a morsel of bread” for his three visitors and then runs to slaughter a calf (Gen 18:5–7). Here the guest asks for the morsel and the host has nothing; it will be God who over-delivers. The KJV’s “as she was going to fetch it” turns two successive actions into one simultaneous action and supplies “it”; the Hebrew has only “she went to take”. Malbim reads the sequence as a probe: Elijah has seen her go home for water, so he knows she lacks none, and asks next for bread. The Hebrew’s repeated “take” (qĕḥî in v. 10, lāqaḥat, liqḥî here) is the scene’s thread, which the KJV’s “fetch … fetch … bring” snips.

philological_notes.note: “Take.” The imperative appears here in a fuller form (liqḥî, with the first consonant of the root kept) than the qĕḥî of v. 10. Radak’s only remark on the verse is that the lamed “stands with a gaʿya” (the small stress mark on the lamed), which I read as a pointing note, not a change of meaning.

“A morsel of bread”: pat is a broken-off piece. Metzudat Zion links it to the verb of Lev 2:6, “break it in pieces” (pātōt). The identical phrase with “take” is Abraham’s modest offer at Mamre (Gen 18:5), which is my own observation.

verses.translation_literal: And she said: Living [is] YHWH your God—if there is to me a cake, except [for] a palm’s fullness of flour in the jar and a little oil in the jug; and here I [am] gathering two sticks, and I will come, and I will make it for me and for my son, and we will eat it, and we will die.
verses.translation_dramatic: And she answered him—and she swore, as he had sworn, by the living LORD: “As the LORD your God lives, I have nothing baked. Nothing. A palmful of flour in the jar, a little oil in the jug—and see, here I am, gathering two sticks. Two. I will go in. I will make it for myself and for my son. We will eat it. And we will die.”
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the low point of the window: a woman who has counted her last meal down to two sticks, a palmful of flour and a little oil. A kaf is the flat of the hand, so “a palm’s fullness” is smaller than a fistful: an ounce or two, a couple of mouthfuls of flat bread, with two twigs just enough to bake one thin cake. Rashi, Radak, Ralbag and Metzudat David gloss “we will die” plainly: after this, nothing. Malbim notes the setup: God sends the prophet when exactly one meal is left, so she qualifies for a miracle. She swears by the LORD, and says “your God”, not “my God”: she knows whose prophet he is, and uses Elijah’s own oath form from v. 1.

The KJV flattens three things. “I have not a cake” turns an oath into a plain denial; the Hebrew is the broken oath again, “if there is to me a cake …”. “Barrel” for kad is anachronistic, for a kad is a pottery jar, the kind Rebekah carries on her shoulder (Gen 24:15), and “cruse” for ṣappaḥat is archaic: Rashi calls it a small bottle and compares Saul’s water flask (1 Sam 26:11). Worst, “that I may go in and dress it … that we may eat it, and die” makes death a purpose. The Hebrew is a flat chain of five verbs, I will come, I will make it, we will eat it, we will die, and the last two end in the same -nû, a slow funeral beat.

philological_notes.note: “A cake”: a baked round, from the root of ʿûgâ, the small cake Elijah asks for next (v. 13). Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it to ʿûgâ; Radak glosses it as any baked piece, large or small. Metzudat Zion cites its one other occurrence, Ps 35:16.
“The fullness of a palm.” kaf is the palm or flat of the hand (Metzudat Zion: “the flat of the hand”), smaller than a fistful. Rashi cites Targum Jonathan’s “the fullness of a hand’s portion”.

“And we will eat it, and we will die.” Two verbs side by side, both first-person plural: the speech ends on death. Rashi and Radak read it as famine death once this food is gone; Malbim adds that her imminent death is what makes her fit for a miracle.

events.title: Elijah declares a drought to King Ahab
events.narrative_summary: Elijah the Tishbite of Gilead tells Ahab, by the living LORD, that there will be no dew or rain in the coming years except by his word.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The chapter gives no year, only Ahab's reign and 'these years' (17:1). The anchor is Ahab's accession, 874 BCE +/- 1 year (Thiele, anchor.ahab_accession). The reign runs to 853 BCE, about 21 years. The start is the midpoint of the reign (offset 10.5 years), and the margin of 10.5 years covers the whole reign, so the window is accession to the end of the reign. Duration: a speech of about ten minutes. Precision MACRO_ERA: the scene is set in a reign with no numbered year; REGNAL_YEAR would need a year number, and 17:1 gives none.

events.title: Elijah is sent east to hide by Cherith
events.narrative_summary: The word of the LORD tells Elijah to go east and hide by the brook Cherith, facing the Jordan. Elijah goes and dwells there.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The command comes right after the declaration: 17:2 follows 17:1 with no interval. The start is the end of the declaration, give or take a day (margin 1 day, no offset). Duration: the going east, one day on foot from Gilead to Cherith (urim travel: 25 km straight, about 31 km by road, walk at 4 km/h, 1 day elapsed). The packet's 'from here' (17:3) is where Elijah stands before Ahab, and Ahab's court is not named, so the journey is measured from Gilead, Elijah's home district; a leg from the court itself may be longer. The command and the going (17:2–5) are one event: the text marks no gap between 'go' and 'so he went'. Precision DAY_SEQUENCE: only order is given.

events.title: Elijah lives by the brook, fed by ravens
events.narrative_summary: Ravens bring Elijah bread and meat in the morning and in the evening, and he drinks from the brook. The event covers the whole stay until the brook dries.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The stay starts right after the arrival at Cherith, give or take half a day (margin 12 hours, no offset). The text gives no interval, but the first meal comes at the next morning or evening, so the start can be up to twelve hours after arrival. The text gives no length for the stay: 17:7 says only 'after a while', literally 'at the end of days'. Six months is a placeholder, not a figure from the text, and the packet has no commentary on that phrase; its uncertainty is carried by the margin of brook_dries_up. The meals repeat daily, so this event stands for the whole stay, not one meal. Precision DAY_SEQUENCE: the meals are daily and undated. The word of 17:4 ('I have commanded the ravens to feed you there') comes true here (17:6).
events.ancient_diurnal_marker: In the morning and in the evening

events.title: The brook at Cherith dries up
events.narrative_summary: The brook Cherith dries up because there has been no rain in the land. The drying is the sign that the drought has reached Elijah's refuge.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Anchored on the end of the stay (fed_by_ravens_at_cherith). The start is that end, give or take six months: the margin is the uncertainty of the stay's length, which the text does not give. Duration one day for the drying as a sign. Precision DAY_SEQUENCE: 'at the end of days' counts days without a date.

events.title: Elijah is sent to Zarephath and reaches its gate
events.narrative_summary: The word of the LORD tells Elijah to rise and go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, where a widow has been commanded to feed him. He sets out and arrives at the city gate.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The word comes right after the drying: 17:8 follows 17:7 with no interval. The start is the end of the drying, give or take a day (margin 1 day, no offset), which allows for a delay the text does not mention. Command and departure are one event (17:8–10a): the text marks no gap between 'arise, go' and 'so he arose and went'. Duration: five days on foot from Cherith to Zarephath (urim travel: 122 km straight, about 153 km by road, walk at 4 km/h, 5 days elapsed). Walk mode, because the text gives a command, not a flight. Precision DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Elijah asks the widow for bread and promises a supply
events.narrative_summary: At the gate Elijah asks the widow for water and a morsel of bread. She answers that she has only a handful of meal and a little oil and is gathering wood for a last meal; Elijah tells her to make him a cake first, and promises that the jar and jug will not run out until the LORD sends rain.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The encounter starts right after the arrival at the gate, give or take an hour (margin 1 hour, no offset): 17:10 gives the arrival and the sighting together, with no interval. No time of day is given. Duration: about one hour, for the request, the reply and the promise (17:10–14). The promise of 17:14 (the jar and jug will not fail until the day the LORD sends rain) is fulfilled in the next event, which takes its length from it. Precision DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Elijah lodges with the widow as the meal lasts
events.narrative_summary: For many days Elijah, the widow and her household eat, and the jar and the jug do not run out, as Elijah had said. The widow's son's illness and restoration fall inside this stay.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The stay starts right after the promise, give or take a day (margin 1 day, no offset): 17:15 says she went and did as Elijah said, with no interval. Duration: 'many days' (17:15) has no number in the text. Metzudat Zion on 17:15 glosses 'days' as 'a year' ('our sages of blessed memory said: a year'), so the stay is taken as one year. That is the tradition's count, not the text's own figure. 1 Kings 18:1, outside this chapter, places the summons in the third year of the drought; see the reviewer notes. The promise of 17:14 holds until the rain, so the stay ends with the rain that chapter 18 names. Precision DAY_SEQUENCE. The word of 17:9 ('I have commanded a widow there to sustain you') comes true here (17:15).

events.title: Elijah raises the widow's son to life
events.narrative_summary: The widow's son falls ill until no breath is left in him. After Elijah prays over him three times, the LORD restores the boy's life, and Elijah returns him to his mother, who says she now knows that Elijah is a man of God.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 17:17 'after these things' places the illness inside the stay, but gives no time. The window is the whole one-year stay: the start is its midpoint (offset 0.5 years) and the margin of 0.5 years covers the rest, with no date claimed for the illness. Duration: one day, an estimate, from the illness to the return of the son. Verses 17:17–24 are one scene. Precision DAY_SEQUENCE.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Inferred, not stated: with the brook dry (17:7), the LORD's next word sends Elijah to a new place of provision (17:8–9).
The declared lack of dew and rain (17:1) is fulfilled when the brook dries 'because there had been no rain in the land' (17:7).
The LORD's word, 'I have commanded the ravens to feed you there' (17:4), is fulfilled as the ravens bring Elijah bread and meat (17:6).
The LORD's word, 'I have commanded a widow there to sustain you' (17:9), is fulfilled as the widow sustains Elijah and her household (17:15).
Elijah's promise that the jar and jug will not run out until the LORD sends rain (17:14) is fulfilled as the meal and oil last for many days (17:15–16).

entities.etymology_meaning: Plain nouns: 'kad', a jar or container; 'qemaḥ', fine flour.
entities.summary_bio: The widow's jar of flour, of which only a handful is left when Elijah comes (17:12). By the LORD's word spoken through Elijah, it does not waste or run out until the LORD sends rain (17:14, 17:16).

entities.etymology_meaning: Plain nouns: 'ṣappaḥat', a small jar or flask; 'šemen', oil.
entities.summary_bio: The widow's jug of oil, with only a little left (17:12). Like the meal, it does not fail through the drought, by the word of the LORD (17:14, 17:16).

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably from the verb 'to be' (hāyāh), so 'he is' or 'he causes to be'; scholars differ on the form.
entities.summary_bio: The God of Israel, sworn by in Elijah's oath (17:1) and in the widow's (17:12). He speaks to Elijah, sends him to Cherith and then to Zarephath, promises the widow that her jar and jug will not fail, and hears Elijah's prayer for her son (17:2 to 17:22).

entities.etymology_meaning: The ordinary Hebrew word for ravens (ʿōrēḇ), birds of the crow family.
entities.summary_bio: A flock of birds that the LORD commands to feed Elijah at Cherith. They bring him bread and meat in the morning and in the evening (17:4, 17:6).

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably a cut or ravine, from a root meaning 'to cut'; the name describes the wadi.
entities.summary_bio: A wadi, a seasonal brook, east of the Jordan, where Elijah is told to hide (17:3). He drinks from it and is fed there by ravens until the brook dries up (17:5 to 17:7).

entities.etymology_meaning: Folk etymology in Genesis 31:47 to 31:48 links it to 'heap of witness'; scholars differ on the original meaning.
entities.summary_bio: A mountainous region east of the Jordan. Elijah is one of the resident aliens of Gilead (17:1), the region of his origin.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'the descender', from yārad, 'to go down', for the river's fall toward the Dead Sea.
entities.summary_bio: The river that gives Cherith its position: the brook lies 'before' the Jordan, 'on the face of' it (17:3, 17:5). No event of this chapter takes place at the river.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'fishery' or 'hunting ground', from ṣîḏ, 'to hunt, to fish'; Genesis 10:15 also makes Sidon the firstborn of Canaan.
entities.summary_bio: A city whose region includes Zarephath: Elijah is sent to Zarephath, which belongs to Zidon (17:9). The chapter mentions the city only in that clause.

entities.etymology_meaning: Unknown. The text gives only the gentilic 'the Tishbite' (tišbî).
entities.summary_bio: Elijah's home town, named only through his epithet 'the Tishbite' (17:1). The chapter gives no description of it.

entities.etymology_meaning: From ʿālâ, 'to go up': a room on an upper floor or roof.
entities.summary_bio: The upper room of the widow's house, where Elijah lodges (17:19). He lays the boy on his own bed here, prays, and stretches himself over him three times before bringing him down to his mother (17:19 to 17:23).

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'refining place', from a root meaning to refine or smelt (ṣārap).
entities.summary_bio: A town in the territory of Sidon where Elijah is sent to stay (17:9). He meets the widow at its gate (17:10) and lodges in her house, where the jar and jug do not fail and her son dies and is raised (17:15 to 17:24).

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'father's brother' (ʾāḥ, 'brother', and ʾāb, 'father'); a name, not a title.
entities.summary_bio: The man Elijah confronts in 17:1 with an oath and a word of drought. This chapter names him only there and does not call him king; the wider account of his reign is not yet in the corpus.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'my God is Yah': 'my God' (ʾēlî) with a short form of the divine name (yāh).
entities.summary_bio: A prophet from Tishbe in Gilead. He comes before Ahab with an oath by the LORD and a word of drought, is sent to hide by the brook Cherith and then to Zarephath, where he lodges with a widow. After praying over her son, he raises the boy to life (17:1 to 17:24).

entities.etymology_meaning: Not a name: 'widow' (ʾalmānâ), a woman with no husband. The text gives her no personal name.
entities.summary_bio: A widow in Zarephath with a son, during the drought. Elijah asks her for water and bread at the city gate; she has only a handful of meal and a little oil and expects to die. She feeds Elijah from what she has, and when her son dies she accuses Elijah, then receives the boy back alive and says Elijah is a man of God.

entities.etymology_meaning: Not a name: 'son' (bēn) of the widow; 'lad' (yeled) in 17:21 to 17:23.
entities.summary_bio: The widow's son. He falls sick and stops breathing (17:17). Elijah carries him to the upper room and lays him on Elijah's own bed, and after a prayer the child's breath returns (17:19 to 17:22). Elijah brings him down and gives him back to his mother alive (17:23).

components.evidence_explanation: Told to hide by the brook Cherith (17:3) and dwells there (17:5).
Lodges in the widow's house at Zarephath (17:19), 'the widow with whom I sojourn' (17:20).
Elijah swears by the LORD 'before whom I stand' (17:1).
She has 'an handful of meal in a barrel' (17:12).
She has 'a little oil in a cruse' (17:12).
She expects that she and her son will eat the last meal and die (17:12). Inferred from her words; her mood is not named.
Her son has died, and she accuses Elijah (17:17 to 17:18). Inferred from the text; grief is not named.
'There was no breath left in him' (17:17).
'The soul of the child came into him again, and he revived' (17:22).

systems.name: The word of the LORD sends a prophet
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the prophetic books, 'the word of the LORD came to' a prophet opens a commission. In this chapter the phrase appears twice (17:2, 17:8), and each time it is followed by a destination.
rules_and_mechanics: The word comes to the prophet unbidden and names a place or a task (17:3, 17:9).
The prophet goes at once and does what the word says (17:5, 17:10).

systems.name: Drought declared by a prophet's word
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Rain and dew were understood as the gift of the god who governed the weather. A drought was read as that god's judgment, and a prophet who could announce it spoke with the god's authority.
rules_and_mechanics: The prophet swears by the living LORD before declaring the withholding (17:1).
The prophet's word sets the length of the drought, not a fixed term (17:1). It ends only when the LORD gives rain (17:14).

systems.name: Oath by the living LORD
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Swearing 'as the LORD lives' calls the god to witness the truth of what is said. It is a solemn speech form in Israel, and here both a prophet and a poor widow use it.
rules_and_mechanics: The formula names the LORD as living and as the God of Israel (17:1) or as the speaker's God (17:12).
The oath is sworn to the person who is to hear or act on the words (17:1 to Ahab; 17:12 to Elijah).

systems.name: Raising the dead by prophetic prayer
systems.ancient_near_east_context: The chapter gives no ritual formula. The act is intercession and bodily contact: the prophet prays aloud and lies over the child, and the returning breath is ascribed to the LORD.
rules_and_mechanics: The prophet prays aloud to the LORD and asks that the child's life return (17:21).
He stretches himself over the child three times (17:21).
The LORD hears the prophet's voice and the breath returns to the child (17:22).

systems.name: Supernatural provision in famine
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Food in a famine is the test of a god's care. The chapter has the LORD feed a prophet through birds and sustain a widow's household from a small jar and jug.
rules_and_mechanics: Provision comes through means the text names: ravens at Cherith (17:4, 17:6), and a jar and jug at Zarephath (17:14, 17:16).
The jar and jug do not run out for the length of the drought; they fail only on the day the LORD sends rain (17:14, 17:16).

system_instances.outcome_summary: Elijah stretches himself over the dead boy three times and cries to the LORD; the child's breath returns and he lives.
system_instances.significance_note: The only revival in the chapter, and the sign the widow recognizes. It leads her to call Elijah a man of God.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Elijah declares that no dew or rain will fall in these years except by his word.
system_instances.significance_note: The chapter's central claim: the prophet's word controls the rain. The brook, the widow and the meal all depend on this act.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Elijah swears by the living LORD before whom he stands, and the oath governs the drought he announces.
system_instances.significance_note: The oath gives the declaration its authority and roots Elijah's standing in his service to the LORD.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The jar of meal and the jug of oil do not waste or fail, and the household eats for many days.
system_instances.significance_note: The chapter's main provision miracle. The LORD sustains a widow's household through the drought, by the word Elijah spoke.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Ravens bring Elijah bread and meat in the morning and in the evening, and he drinks from the brook.
system_instances.significance_note: The first provision miracle. It comes without human agency and prepares for the second one at Zarephath.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The widow swears by the living LORD her God that she has only a handful of meal and a little oil, and that she and her son expect to die.
system_instances.significance_note: Her oath confirms the scarcity that Elijah's miracle must overcome, and it sets up the promise that follows.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The word of the LORD sends Elijah east to hide by the brook Cherith, and he goes and dwells there.
system_instances.significance_note: The first commission in the chapter. It removes the prophet from Ahab's reach, and the same word arranges his food through the ravens.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The word sends Elijah to Zarephath to stay with a widow whom the LORD has already prepared.
system_instances.significance_note: The second commission. The widow is commanded before Elijah arrives, so the meeting at the gate is arranged rather than chanced.

edges.description: Elijah asks the widow to bring him a little water and then a morsel of bread from her hand.
Elijah goes and does what the LORD said, and he dwells by the brook.
Elijah cries to the LORD, asks whether the LORD has brought evil on the widow, and stretches himself over the child three times.
Elijah swears by the LORD and declares that there will be no dew or rain in these years except by his word.
Elijah carries the boy down from the upper room, gives him to his mother, and says that her son lives.
The ravens bring Elijah bread and meat in the morning and in the evening, and he drinks from the brook.
When her son falls ill, the widow asks Elijah what she has to do with him and whether he came to bring her sin to remembrance.
She goes and makes Elijah a small cake first, as he said, and the household eats for many days.
The widow declares that Elijah is a man of God and that the word of the LORD in his mouth is truth.
The word of the LORD tells Elijah to go east and hide by the brook Cherith.
The LORD sends Elijah to Zarephath, which belongs to Zidon, to stay with a widow.
The LORD tells Elijah that he has commanded the ravens to feed him at Cherith.
Through Elijah, the LORD promises that the jar of meal and the jug of oil will not fail until the day the LORD gives rain.
The jar and jug do not waste or fail, according to the LORD's word spoken by Elijah.
The LORD hears Elijah's voice, the child's breath returns, and he lives.
